passages.happening:
The chapter opens with a rule about offerings. No ox or sheep ‘with any defect or serious flaw’ may be sacrificed to God (verse 1).

Then comes a case for the courts. A man or woman in one of Israel's towns is found ‘going to worship other gods’, or the sun, moon or stars (verses 2-3). When it is reported, ‘you must investigate it thoroughly’ (verse 4). If it is true, the person is to be brought out to the town gate and stoned to death (verse 5).

The law then sets a limit. “On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death, but he shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness” (verse 6). “The hands of the witnesses shall be the first in putting him to death, and after that, the hands of all the people” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the same offense as in chapter 13, seen from the side of the court. There the stress was on those who urge others toward other gods. Here it is on how a charge must be handled.

The town gate was Israel's courthouse. The elders sat there, business was witnessed there, and sentences were carried out just outside it.

Notice that the law names ‘a man or woman’. Women were held responsible before God's covenant as men were.

The weight of the passage falls on its safeguards. First, a report must be looked into thoroughly. A rumor may not be acted on. Second, no one may be put to death on one person's word. One witness could be an enemy, a liar or simply mistaken. Third, the witnesses must throw the first stones. That made an accusation costly. A person who lied under oath would have to act on the lie with his own hands, before the whole town.

Jewish tradition went further in the same direction. The rabbis built safeguards around capital cases that made a death sentence very hard to reach.

The penalty itself is hard for a modern reader, and the hard question below takes it up. It belongs to Israel as a nation in covenant with God as its king, where the worship of other gods was treated as treason.
passages.later:
This book states the rule of witnesses again for every kind of case: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Jesus applies it to a quarrel between two of his followers: ‘every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses’ (Matthew 18:16). Paul applies it to charges against church leaders: “Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19).

When a woman was brought to Jesus to be stoned, he turned the rule about the first stone on her accusers: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7).
passages.hard:
Why does the law set death as the penalty for worshiping other gods?

To a modern reader, putting someone to death for religious belief is what persecution means. The question deserves a straight answer.

Deuteronomy treats Israel as a nation in covenant with God, with the LORD as its king. In that nation, to worship other gods was treason against the ruler and a danger to the whole people's life in the land. The law also holds the penalty back. It requires careful investigation and two or three witnesses, and it puts the first responsibility on the witnesses.

Christians have read these laws in different ways. Most traditions hold that the penalties belonged to Israel as a political nation under the old covenant and do not pass to the church, which bears no sword. The New Testament's parallel is exclusion from the church's fellowship, not execution (1 Corinthians 5). A smaller group, sometimes called theonomists, argues that Israel's civil laws still offer a model for governments today. Most Reformed churches have rejected that position.

The note on chapter 13, verses 1 to 5, says what must be said here too. No church and no state may use this law against anyone. Christians have at times used chapters like this to justify persecution, and that was a grave misreading.
passages.asks: The law would not let one voice destroy a person. Ask how many voices you need before you believe the worst about someone, and whether you have ever passed on a charge you had from one source only. And think of the first stone. Ask whether you would still accuse if you had to carry out the consequences yourself, in front of everyone.

passages.t: When a case is too hard
passages.happening:
Some cases will be beyond a local court: questions of ‘bloodshed, lawsuits, or assaults’ (verse 8). Then the judges are to go up to the place God chooses and bring the case ‘to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time’ (verse 9).

The ruling given there is final. “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you” (verse 11).

A man who ‘acts presumptuously’ and refuses to listen to the priest or the judge is to be put to death (verse 12). “Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 16 put judges in every town. This law adds a higher court at the central sanctuary for the cases a town could not settle. The examples are the hard ones. One is whether a killing was murder or an accident. Others are disputes over rights and cases of injury.

The court joins priests and a judge. The priests knew God's law. The judge knew how to weigh a case. Difficult questions were to be decided by people who knew both.

The words ‘at that time’ are worth noticing. The law does not name a person. It names an office. Whoever holds it in a given generation is to be heard.

The severe penalty of verse 12 is not for an honest mistake or for disagreement. The word ‘presumptuously’ describes a person who acts in open, proud defiance of the court's ruling. A community cannot have justice if anyone may set a verdict aside because he does not like it. The law is protecting the court on which every weak person depends.

This is a law about Israel's courts in the land. It is not a rule that religious leaders must never be questioned. The same book says that the king himself is under the law, and that a prophet who speaks falsely is not to be feared.
passages.later:
King Jehoshaphat later set up such a court in Jerusalem, of Levites, priests and heads of families, ‘to judge on behalf of the LORD and to settle disputes’ (2 Chronicles 19:8).

The picture of not turning ‘to the right or to the left’ is used of the whole people at Sinai (Deuteronomy 5:32), here of those who receive a verdict, and a few verses later of the king himself (verse 20).
passages.asks: Israel was to carry its hardest questions to people who knew both God's law and the facts. Ask whom you go to when a matter is too hard for you, and whether you choose advisers for their wisdom or because they will agree with you. And ask how you respond to a fair decision that goes against you.

passages.happening:
Moses looks ahead to a day when Israel, settled in the land, will say, ‘Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us’ (verse 14). It may have a king, on conditions.

He must be the one God chooses, and one of their own people (verse 15).

Three things he must not pile up. “But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses” (verse 16). “He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray. He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold” (verse 17).

One thing he must do. “When he is seated on his royal throne, he must write for himself a copy of this instruction on a scroll in the presence of the Levitical priests. It is to remain with him, and he is to read from it all the days of his life” (verses 18-19).

The purpose is given. “Then his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen, and he will not turn aside from the commandment, to the right or to the left” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Kingship was the normal form of government across the ancient world. Kings in Egypt and Mesopotamia were often presented as sons of the gods or as the source of law. Against that background this law is striking.

Israel's king does not make the law. He receives it. He is chosen by God, he must be a brother Israelite, and he is given no power in this passage except the duty to read.

The three things forbidden were the three marks of royal greatness.

Horses in this period were not farm animals. They were used for chariots in war, and Egypt was a known source of them. A king who gathered horses was building a standing army and trusting in it.

Many wives usually meant marriages made for the sake of alliances with foreign royal houses. Each wife brought her own gods.

Great stores of silver and gold meant heavy taxes and forced labor for the people who supplied them.

So the law takes from the king the army, the alliances and the treasury that other kings relied on. What it gives him in their place is a scroll. He is to write out his own copy of the law by hand, with the priests watching, keep it by him, and read it every day. The ruler is to be a student of a text he did not write.

The Greek translation of the words ‘a copy of this instruction’ rendered them as a second law. That phrase gave this book its English name.

The last verse says what the reading is for. It is to keep the king's heart from being lifted ‘above his countrymen’. Verse 15 has already called them his brothers. In Israel the king is a brother among brothers, walking the same road as the poorest of them, with the same warning not to turn aside.
passages.later:
Israel did ask for a king, in the words Moses foresaw: “Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations” (1 Samuel 8:5).

King Solomon did all three things the law forbids. “Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses”, and his horses ‘were imported from Egypt’ (1 Kings 10:26, 28). “The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones” (1 Kings 10:27). And ‘he had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines’, who ‘turned his heart away’ (1 Kings 11:3). The writers of Kings seem to have had this chapter open before them.

The prophet Zechariah looked for a different kind of king, ‘humble and riding on a donkey’ (Zechariah 9:9). Matthew says that Jesus entered Jerusalem in that way (Matthew 21:5). The New Testament presents him as the king this law longs for. The law itself makes no prediction.

Jesus taught his followers the same thing about power: “whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant” (Mark 10:43).
passages.asks: The law took from the king what makes rulers feel safe and gave him a book to read. Ask what you rely on to feel secure and in control, and what place God's word has beside it. And if you have authority over anyone, at work, at home or in a church, ask whether your heart has been lifted above them. The king was to remember that his subjects were his brothers.
